Q: Difference between CONCAT with II and CONCAT with + A:

Different RDBMS have their own SQL dialects, some use || and some use +.

|| is ANSI SQL.

Note many RDBMS also provide a CONCAT function as an option.

Q: Xslt 1.0 check if something exists or empty value? A:

The XPath 1.0 specification states that:

• a string is true if and only if its length is non-zero

Therefore the expression:

boolean(string)

returns false when string is empty, true otherwise.

Conversely, the expression:

not(string)

returns true when string is empty, false otherwise.

Note that there is no need to convert the string explicitly to a boolean when used within the test attribute of xsl:if or xsl:choose. You can do simply:

<xsl:if test="string">
   <!-- do something when string is not empty -->
</xsl:if>

Q: Is there a feature (pattern synonyms?) to turn a datatype into syntactic sugar for constructing another datatype? A:

How about using a custom type error for the matches?

module Internal where
import GHC.TypeLits

class PatternNotPermitted (a :: Symbol)
data Bar = Bar (Bool -> Int -> Bool -> String)
pattern Foo :: PatternNotPermitted "Foo" => () => String -> Bar
pattern Foo x <- (undefined -> x) where Foo a = Bar (\_ _ _ -> a)

module External (Bar(..)) where
import GHC.TypeLits
import Internal

instance TypeError (Text "The " :<>: Text a :<>: " pattern is for construction only") => PatternNotPermitted a

Try it out in ghci:

External> let Foo x = undefined
<interactive>:1:5: error: [GHC-64725]
    • The Foo pattern is for construction only
    • In the pattern: Foo x
      In a pattern binding: Foo x = undefined

Q: Is it safe to reuse UserDetails from SecurityContext instead of querying the database again? A:

It is safe to reuse the UserDetails from the SecurityContext because the user information has already been loaded from the database and is considered valid for the duration of the request. Additionally, as you mentioned, making multiple database calls to load the same user information would be inefficient.

A couple of additional points:

  1. You can introduce caching in your application to reduce database calls if user data needs to be loaded from the database in other parts of the application.

  2. If you are using JPA/Hibernate, it already provides a persistence context (first-level cache). Within the same persistence context, Hibernate avoids reloading the same entity multiple times.

Q: Should I use AI to learn? A:

Personally, I find the skill of "research" to be very important. As a beginner, I think it's important to develop your research skills while it's easier and there is more information available. This involves browsing documentation, asking questions on forums, consulting more experienced developers, etc. As you advance in your programming journey, you'll encounter more advanced topics--things which AI will barf complete nonsense about--so it's very important to build a foundation on how to independently (without AI, I mean) develop your answers.

Also, be very mindful not to offload all your critical thinking onto AI. Honestly, it's very easy to do so. Use it as someone to talk about your ideas with. I sometimes use AI like those "rubber duck" debuggers when I am stuck. You're still doing most of the thinking; AI is just a listener.

You shouldn't avoid AI altogether, though. That would just be hindering your progression for no reason. For example, I've found it to be extremely good at explaining IL or assembly, and I use it often for that. I'll also use it to brainstorm ideas, which I then assess independently one-by-one. I'll also use it to expose myself to more advanced or niche concepts. These LLMs have seen a lot of things. Their detail in these topics may not be accurate (and you have to fact-check yourself), but that exposure is still very nice. AI is also very effective at generating boilerplate or use-and-discard tests.

My take on AI, though: use it as a vessel to develop your skills. Naturally, as you become more advanced, your usage and goals with AI will change. Sorry if the advice is very broad. These are just my thoughts on the topic.

Q: bash script error converting zip file to tar.gz (or tar.bz2) A:

Try this script (named zip-to-tar, tested on Ubuntu):

#!/bin/bash
dir=$(mktemp -d) file=$(realpath $2)
if test "${file##*.}" = gz; then
    flag=z
elif test "${file##*.}" = bz2; then
    flag=j
else
    echo "Unknow extension in filename [$2]."
fi
unzip "$1" -d "$dir" && tar ${flag}cvf "$file" -C "$dir" .
rm -rf "$dir"
# example : zip-to-tar test.zip /tmp/test.tar.gz
# example : zip-to-tar test.zip /tmp/test.tar.bz2
